title: The handling party for a technical issue must not be the Core Facilitator wherever there is a non-trivial chance they would downplay it
content:
A.1.10.2.4.7.3.3 designates a handling party for each technical issue: "This party will typically be the Core Facilitator. However, if there is a **non-trivial chance** that the Core Facilitator will ignore or downplay the issue, another entity should serve as the handling party."

The threshold is the provision's whole substance. Not evidence of misconduct, not credible suspicion of compromise — a non-trivial chance of *downplaying*. That covers ordinary conflicts of interest: an issue caused by the Facilitator's own instruction, one whose resolution would delay a Spell they are accountable for, or one implicating a party they work with daily.

The reason for such a low bar is structural. The Core Facilitator holds the binding decision on Spell inclusion (A.1.10.2.4.3.1.3.1) and also follows up to confirm issues are resolved (A.1.10.2.4.7.3.5). Routing an issue about the Facilitator's own process to the Facilitator makes them judge in their own cause, and the failure mode is not dramatic suppression but quiet reprioritization — which is exactly what "ignore or downplay" names.

Note who decides: the discovering party, not the Facilitator. Whoever found the issue chooses the handler, so the person with the conflict cannot claim jurisdiction over their own case. Together with A.1.10.2.4.3.1.3.1's compromised-Facilitator clause, a pattern emerges — every concentration of authority in this process ships with a pre-specified condition for bypassing it.
description: A.1.10.2.4.7.3.3 sets a deliberately low bar for bypassing the default handler, requiring no proof of bad faith — only a plausible conflict of interest in the outcome.
